title: The same SQL, three databases
summary: Port an upsert across PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite while keeping the behavior explicit.

scenario.briefing: A players table is moving from a MySQL prototype to PostgreSQL, and the same file also runs against SQLite in local tests. The team keeps assuming that SQL that parses everywhere means the same thing everywhere.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Review an artifact and identify the concrete risks.

hints: PostgreSQL uses GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY for an identity column.
PostgreSQL and SQLite use ON CONFLICT (column) DO UPDATE; MySQL uses ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
Only PostgreSQL and SQLite 3.35+ have RETURNING; MySQL needs a follow-up SELECT or LAST_INSERT_ID.
Booleans are BOOLEAN, TINYINT(1), and INTEGER in the three databases; all three accept LIMIT.

misconceptions.description: Assuming identical SQL text has identical behavior everywhere.
misconceptions.feedback: Collation, uniqueness, and ordering rules differ. Accepting the query hides portability bugs.

misconceptions.description: Using PostgreSQL upsert syntax in MySQL.
misconceptions.testDescription: The MySQL variant uses AUTO_INCREMENT and ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
misconceptions.feedback: MySQL uses ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, not ON CONFLICT. Keep dialect-specific files explicit.

misconceptions.testDescription: The SQLite variant uses AUTOINCREMENT, integer booleans, and RETURNING.
misconceptions.feedback: Modern SQLite supports RETURNING. The differences that matter are AUTOINCREMENT, type affinity, and boolean storage.

sections.title: A shared grammar hides different rules
sections.body: A statement can parse on PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite and still compare, sort, or constrain values differently. Collation decides whether email comparisons are case-sensitive and whether case variants collide in a unique index.

sections.title: Upserts and RETURNING
sections.body: PostgreSQL and SQLite use ON CONFLICT (column) DO UPDATE. MySQL uses ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE and has no RETURNING. SQLite gained RETURNING in 3.35; MySQL needs a follow-up SELECT or LAST_INSERT_ID.

sections.title: Identity, booleans, and LIMIT
sections.body: PostgreSQL uses GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, MySQL uses AUTO_INCREMENT, and SQLite uses INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT. Booleans are native BOOLEAN, TINYINT(1), and INTEGER 0/1. All three accept LIMIT, but without ORDER BY the surviving rows are unspecified.

steps.title: Port the player upsert
steps.prompt: Edit dialects.sql. Write the PostgreSQL table and upsert for players.handle, return the stored row, and record the MySQL 8 and SQLite 3.35 equivalents as comments. Note the identity, boolean, and LIMIT differences.

tests.description: PostgreSQL uses an identity column and a native boolean.
includes: id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE

tests.description: The PostgreSQL upsert targets handle and returns the stored row.
The MySQL variant uses AUTO_INCREMENT and ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
includes: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE email = incoming.email

tests.description: The SQLite variant uses AUTOINCREMENT, integer booleans, and RETURNING.
The file states the LIMIT rule and avoids SELECT *.
includes: LIMIT exists in all three dialects
id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY

hints: Separate portable SQL from vendor-specific syntax.
Check identity, boolean, and upsert syntax in each dialect.
Verify what each database returns from an upsert.
Use identity/boolean in PostgreSQL, AUTO_INCREMENT/ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE in MySQL, and AUTOINCREMENT/RETURNING in SQLite.

steps.title: Review the cross-database query
steps.prompt: Review the artifact and select every real portability problem.

artifact.title: email-lookup.sql
artifact.caption: The application sends this query to PostgreSQL and MySQL. users.email is VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE on both databases. PostgreSQL uses the C collation; MySQL 8 uses utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci.
artifact.content:
-- The application sends this query to PostgreSQL and MySQL.
SELECT id, email
FROM users
WHERE email = 'Ada@Example.com'
ORDER BY email
LIMIT 10;

findings.label: MySQL's default collation compares email case-insensitively, so the filter can match rows PostgreSQL would not.
The UNIQUE constraint enforces different rules: MySQL's default collation rejects case variants that PostgreSQL accepts.
ORDER BY email can return a different order because the databases sort with different collations.
LIMIT 10 is the portability problem because MySQL and SQLite do not support LIMIT.
SQLite rejects VARCHAR(255), so the schema cannot be ported.

verdicts.label: Block the change until collation and uniqueness behavior are tested per dialect.
Ship it; identical syntax guarantees identical results.

steps.explanation: The statements parse on both engines but compare and sort differently. Pin the collation, test the unique constraint behavior, and set explicit ORDER BY expectations for each dialect.
hints: Find assumptions that depend on collation or dialect.
Check whether ORDER BY is deterministic across databases.
Ask whether LIMIT without ORDER BY is stable.
Block the query: collation, uniqueness, and ordering differ across engines.
